title: Financially stressed adults seek guidance through closer networks and AI while trust in AI remains low
source_unit: Gallup and Edward Jones survey of US and Canadian adults seeking financial guidance in the prior year
geography: United States and Canada; US comparisons retained as the primary unit

observations.period: 2026; US adults seeking financial guidance in the prior year

denominator.unit: US adults who sought financial guidance; source does not expose the full unweighted US respondent denominator in the article

any_guidance.unit: percent of US adults reporting at least one financial-guidance source

internet_research.unit: percent of US guidance-seekers using their own internet research

family.unit: percent of US guidance-seekers using family members

professional_advisor.unit: percent of US guidance-seekers using professional financial advisors

ai_guidance.unit: percent of US guidance-seekers using AI tools

observations.method: Gallup/Edward Jones survey comparison of reported financial-guidance sources and confidence; source-specific denominators and question wording are retained rather than pooled.
observations.uncertainty: The article does not provide an account-level sequence from a financial problem to guidance, recommendation, decision, loss, recovery, or later trust; source use is self-reported.
observations.subgroup: US adults who sought financial guidance, with separate generational and financial-fulfillment comparisons.
observations.counterinterpretation: Internet research may be a first step before professional or family consultation, and AI use may supplement rather than replace human advice; use frequency does not identify decision influence.

denominator.unit: US financial-guidance seekers grouped by Gallup/Edward Jones financial fulfillment categories

any_guidance_fulfilled.unit: percent among financially fulfilled US adults

any_guidance_conflicted.unit: percent among financially conflicted US adults

any_guidance_stressed.unit: percent among financially stressed US adults

family_stressed_vs_fulfilled.value: 43% of financially stressed guidance-seekers used family, versus 19% of financially fulfilled guidance-seekers

ai_stressed_vs_fulfilled.value: 21% of financially stressed guidance-seekers used AI, versus 15% of financially fulfilled guidance-seekers

observations.method: Descriptive subgroup comparison using Gallup/Edward Jones financial-fulfillment categories; the source defines fulfillment around security, control, confidence, and alignment with life goals, not income alone.
observations.uncertainty: Financial fulfillment, stress, source use, and confidence are measured in the same survey; the comparison does not establish that stress caused AI or family use, or that guidance improved fulfillment.
observations.subgroup: US financially fulfilled, conflicted, and stressed adults who sought guidance.
observations.counterinterpretation: Stressed adults may use more sources because they have greater need, not because those sources are more effective; family and AI use can coexist with professional advice and internet research.

observations.period: 2026; confidence in guidance sources among US adults

denominator.unit: US adults evaluating financial-guidance sources; source reports broad confidence comparisons

ai_some_confidence.value: no more than 30% of US adults report at least some confidence in AI's financial expertise; 3% report a great deal

younger_ai_confidence.value: 36% of US millennials and 32% of Gen Z adults report at least some confidence, versus 27% of Gen X and 15% of baby boomers

trusted_alternatives.value: finance professors, family members, and friends or colleagues receive higher confidence than AI in the article's comparison

observations.method: Published Gallup comparison of reported use and confidence by source and generation.
observations.uncertainty: Confidence does not measure accuracy, advice quality, financial outcome, or whether a respondent acted on guidance; source rankings may reflect familiarity, access, or social trust.
observations.subgroup: US adults overall and generational groups; AI users and guidance-seekers are not interchangeable universes.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low confidence can coexist with experimentation when AI is cheap, available, or useful for preliminary research; high confidence in family or professionals does not guarantee good advice.

boundary: This record establishes a financial-guidance source mix, financial-stress differences, and low AI confidence. It does not establish recommendation quality, financial decision influence, affordability improvement, harm, human substitution, or later trust, switching, or recovery.
